title: CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE CONCUBINES?
paragraphs:
CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE CONCUBINES?
The Bible’s Answer Is More Uncomfortable Than Many Want to Admit
David had them.
Solomon had hundreds of women.
Abraham had Hagar.
Jacob had Bilhah and Zilpah.
And all of them appear in the Bible.
So here is the question that makes some Christians uncomfortable:
If men in Scripture had concubines, can a Christian have concubines today?
Before you answer too quickly, there is something you need to understand about the Bible.
The Bible is brutally honest about human beings.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not hide Abraham's failures.
It does not erase Jacob's dysfunctional household.
It does not protect David's reputation.
It does not rewrite Solomon's compromises to make him look more spiritual.
Scripture often tells you what happened without telling you to imitate what happened.
And confusing biblical description with biblical permission can lead a person into devastating error.
That distinction matters enormously here.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh.

A concubine in the ancient world was not simply identical to the modern idea of a secret girlfriend or casual sexual partner. The precise legal and social arrangements varied, but generally she occupied a recognized relationship of lower status than a primary wife. Scripture records such relationships in the patriarchal and monarchical worlds.
But recording something is not the same thing as calling it God's ideal.
The Bible records drunkenness.
The Bible records incest.
The Bible records polygamy.
The Bible records adultery.
The Bible records murder.
The Bible records kings doing horrific things.
Nobody reads those accounts and concludes, “It happened to someone in the Bible, therefore God approves of it.”
So when someone says, “But Abraham had Hagar,” the real question is not whether Abraham did it.
He did.
The real question is:
Was Abraham's household arrangement the pattern Jesus gave His followers for marriage?
That changes everything.
Go back before Abraham.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings.
Go all the way back to creation.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression for “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely two people occupying the same household.
Not a powerful man collecting women around himself.
Not a husband keeping one woman as his official wife while maintaining additional sexual partners.
There is covenantal union.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously important.
He went back to Genesis.
Jesus said:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
— Matthew 19:4–6
Jesus did not point His hearers to Solomon's household.
He pointed them to creation.
That should stop us.
Because sometimes we search the Bible looking for the lowest arrangement we can defend when Jesus is calling us back to the highest design God revealed.
There is a difference between asking:
“What did fallen people sometimes do?”
and asking:
“What does Christ call me to do?”
Those are not the same question.
And this is where the issue becomes personal.
Because maybe you are not really asking about an ancient concubine.
Maybe the word is different in your life.
Maybe it is “side relationship.”
Maybe it is “second woman.”
Maybe it is “friends with benefits.”
Maybe it is someone you sleep with while insisting that technically you are not committing adultery.
Maybe it is a relationship hidden from your spouse.
Maybe it is a person you keep emotionally and sexually available while refusing covenant faithfulness.
Maybe nobody calls her a concubine.
But you know she is occupying a place in your life that does not belong to her.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
Changing the vocabulary does not change what God sees.
The New Testament brings Christian sexual ethics into even sharper focus.
Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 7:2
The Greek is striking:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω
hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō, kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
In context, Paul directs each man toward his own wife and each woman toward her own husband.
Christian sexuality is not built around accumulating sexual access.
It is shaped by covenant faithfulness, holiness, self-giving love, and belonging to Christ.
Paul tells the Thessalonian believers:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
— 1 Thessalonians 4:3
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία — porneia, a broad term for sexual immorality.
Then Paul says something our sexually saturated culture desperately needs to hear:
“For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.”
— 1 Thessalonians 4:7
Holiness.
Not technical loopholes.
Not, “How many relationships can I justify?”
Not, “Which Old Testament man can I use as precedent?”
The Christian question is:
“How can my body, marriage, sexuality, and relationships belong completely to Jesus Christ?”

Even the qualifications given for Christian overseers reflect marital fidelity. Paul speaks of being μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra — commonly rendered “the husband of one wife” in 1 Timothy 3:2.

Scholars discuss the precise scope of that expression—whether its emphasis is specifically monogamy, marital faithfulness, or being a “one-woman man.” We should not pretend an interpretive discussion does not exist.
But none of the credible possibilities turns the phrase into permission for maintaining concubines.
The direction is toward fidelity.
That direction becomes even clearer when marriage is placed beside Christ Himself.
Ephesians 5 does not present marriage merely as a convenient human contract.
Christian marriage points beyond itself.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
— Ephesians 5:25
Think about that.
Christ does not teach husbands to use women.
Christ teaches husbands to imitate a Savior who gives Himself.
Christ does not turn marriage into a monument to male appetite.
He turns it into a picture of sacrificial love.
This is why the biblical stories involving multiple wives and concubines should sober us rather than provide excuses.
Look at the fruit.
Abraham's decision involving Hagar produced anguish within his household. Genesis 16 records jealousy, conflict, harsh treatment, and Hagar fleeing into the wilderness.
Jacob's household became consumed by rivalry between Leah and Rachel, with their servants Bilhah and Zilpah drawn into the struggle for children and affection.
David's family became a landscape of sexual sin, violence, rivalry, betrayal, and grief.
And Solomon?
Scripture could hardly be clearer:
“But king Solomon loved many strange women…”
— 1 Kings 11:1
Then:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods…”
— 1 Kings 11:4
The man famous for wisdom still discovered that possessing wisdom is not the same as obeying it.
That should terrify anyone using Solomon's relationships as permission.
His women were not presented at the end of his story as proof that God approved of multiplying partners.
They became part of the account of his heart turning away.
God had already warned Israel's kings:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away…”
— Deuteronomy 17:17
So can a Christian have concubines?

If by “concubine” we mean maintaining additional women as sexual partners alongside or outside the covenantal faithfulness of marriage, that practice cannot be reconciled with the sexual ethic Jesus and the apostles give Christ's followers.
The existence of concubines in biblical history does not establish concubinage as Christian discipleship.
But please don't stop reading here.
Because if you already crossed that line, the Gospel has something to say to you too.
And it is not merely:
“Disgusting. Leave.”
It is:
“Repent. Come home.”
There is a world of difference.
Maybe this article found you while you are already living a double life.
Maybe there is a wife who trusts you and another woman whose messages you delete.
Maybe there is a husband who does not know.
Maybe there are relationships you have carefully renamed because calling them what they really are would force you to confront them.
Maybe you have been using Abraham, David, or Solomon as theological camouflage for something your conscience has already been warning you about.
You do not need a better excuse.
You need Jesus.
And that is not condemnation without hope.
That is precisely where hope begins.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally spotless people congratulating themselves.
It is the story of sinners being rescued by a spotless Savior.
Jesus did not die because our sin was insignificant.
He died because our sin was so serious that reconciliation with God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
At the cross, Christ carried sin.
At the empty tomb, death lost its claim.
And now the invitation is not to hide more intelligently.
It is to repent.
The Greek word so closely associated with repentance is μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because you were exposed.
It is a genuine turning—a changed mind that bears fruit in a changed direction.
You stop defending what Christ calls you to surrender.
You stop making peace with what is destroying your soul.
You stop asking Scripture to approve the life you already chose and begin allowing Scripture to confront, correct, and reshape you.
And yes, repentance can hurt.
Truth often does before healing begins.
A relationship may have to end.
A confession may have to happen.
Trust may need years of rebuilding.
Pastoral help may be necessary.
Accountability may become uncomfortable.
Consequences do not magically disappear simply because someone says, “God forgive me.”
But grace means your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Look at David.
His sin brought devastating consequences, and Scripture never pretends otherwise.
Yet Psalm 51 records the cry of a shattered man:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
David did not need God to help him justify his desires.
He needed God to make his heart clean.
Maybe that is what you need to pray tonight.
Not:
“God, show me how this relationship might technically be allowed.”
But:
“God, create in me a clean heart.”
There are people reading this who have spent years asking how close they can stand to sin without technically stepping into it.
Jesus offers something better.
Freedom.
Purity.
A clean conscience.
A restored heart.
A life where you no longer need secret passwords, disappearing messages, hidden hotel receipts, carefully constructed lies, or theological excuses.
Imagine sleeping without hiding.
Imagine praying without defending your secret life.
Imagine looking at your spouse without carrying another person in the shadows.
Imagine worshiping God without simultaneously negotiating with the sin you refuse to surrender.
That freedom has a name.
Jesus Christ.
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
— John 8:36
So no, the biblical presence of concubines is not a license for Christians to maintain them.
The Bible is showing us something far greater than permission to repeat the broken patterns of ancient men.
It is showing us why broken people need redemption.
And perhaps that is why their scandals were never edited out.
Because if Scripture contained only flawless people, you might think there was no room in it for you.
Abraham failed.
Jacob's household fractured.
David fell spectacularly.
Solomon compromised despite extraordinary wisdom.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul once persecuted the church.
Yet the Bible keeps pointing beyond flawed human beings to the One who never sinned.
Jesus.
That is where your eyes belong.
Not on David to excuse your lust.
Not on Solomon to defend your relationships.
Not on Abraham to rationalize your choices.
On Christ.
The question was never simply, “What could ancient men get away with?”
The deeper question is:
“Now that I belong to Jesus, what must I surrender so that my life looks more like Him?”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the conviction into shame and run farther from God.
Bring it into the light.
There is no trophy for pretending.

And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual sin, adultery, secret relationships, pornography, betrayal, or a life you thought could never change, your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable, but because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Someone may be one secret relationship away from losing a marriage. Someone may already believe they have sinned too badly to return.
Send this to them.
Christ alone is our Savior, and obedience to Him is far bigger than supporting any particular ministry.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone righteous.
Save what you need to remember.
Share what somebody else desperately needs to read.
And comment if God is dealing with your heart.
Because maybe the most dangerous secret is not the one everybody eventually discovers.
Maybe it is the one you successfully hide long enough to convince yourself that God no longer sees it.
But He sees you.
And astonishingly, in Jesus Christ, the God who sees your scandal is still calling you toward grace.
Not grace that blesses the chains.
Grace that breaks them.
Not grace that gives sin a new name.
Grace that gives the sinner a new life.
Not grace that tells you to remain exactly where you are.
Grace that takes your trembling hand and leads you home.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but it does not get to decide who you become after He does.
